changes.old: ## DropConnect: independent masks on connections Suppose two output units receive the same two inputs. Dropping one input removes that input from both output units. DropConnect can remove its connection to the first unit while keeping its connection to the second. The two procedures therefore produce different random networks, even when they retain the same fraction of scalar values. For a linear layer with weights $W\in\mathbb R^{o\times i}$ and input $x\in\mathbb R^i$, inverted input dropout and inverted DropConnect give $$ y_{\mathrm{input}}=W\left(\frac{m\odot x}{q}\right),\qquad y_{\mathrm{connect}}=\left(\frac{M\odot W}{q}\right)x. $$ Here $q$ is the keep probability, $m$ has $i$ independent Bernoulli entries, and $M$ has $oi$ independent entries. Input dropout uses one mask value for an entire column of $W$; DropConnect samples the entries of that column independently. In both formulas the mean linear output is $Wx$. With $x=(1,1)^T$, $W=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ and $q=0.5$, retaining only the first input gives $(2,6)^T$. Keeping only the diagonal connections gives $(2,8)^T$, which input dropout cannot produce. Enumerating all masks also reveals how the noise differs: | Masked quantity | Possible masks | Mean output | Output covariance | |---|---:|---|---| | Two input coordinates | $2^2=4$ | $(3,7)^T$ | $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}5&11\\11&25\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ | | Four connections | $2^4=16$ | $(3,7)^T$ | $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}5&0\\0&25\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ | The variances of the two outputs agree, but input dropout correlates their fluctuations because both outputs lose the same input. Independent connection masks remove that covariance for this fixed linear layer. ```python from itertools import product import math import torch dc_W = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]], dtype=torch.float64) dc_x = torch.ones(2, dtype=dc_W.dtype) dc_q = .5 dc_inputs = torch.tensor(list(product([0., 1.], repeat=2)), dtype=dc_W.dtype) dc_edges = torch.tensor(list(product([0., 1.], repeat=4)), dtype=dc_W.dtype).reshape(-1, 2, 2) dc_y_input = (dc_inputs * dc_x / dc_q) @ dc_W.T dc_y_edges = ((dc_edges * dc_W / dc_q) @ dc_x) def dc_covariance(outputs): centered = outputs - outputs.mean(0) return centered.T @ centered / len(outputs) torch.testing.assert_close(dc_y_input.mean(0), dc_W @ dc_x) torch.testing.assert_close(dc_y_edges.mean(0), dc_W @ dc_x) torch.testing.assert_close(dc_covariance(dc_y_input), torch.tensor([[5., 11.], [11., 25.]], dtype=dc_W.dtype)) torch.testing.assert_close(dc_covariance(dc_y_edges), torch.diag(torch.tensor([5., 25.], dtype=dc_W.dtype))) dc_parameter = dc_W.clone().requires_grad_() dc_diagonal = torch.eye(2, dtype=dc_W.dtype) ((dc_diagonal * dc_parameter / dc_q) @ dc_x).sum().backward() torch.testing.assert_close(dc_parameter.grad, 2 * dc_diagonal) torch.testing.assert_close(dc_parameter.detach(), dc_W) # Original, non-inverted convention: four equiprobable connection masks. dc_z = dc_inputs @ torch.tensor([1., -1.], dtype=dc_W.dtype) assert torch.relu(dc_z).mean().item() == .25 assert torch.relu(dc_z.mean()).item() == 0. dc_gaussian_relu_mean = math.sqrt(.5) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi) assert abs(dc_gaussian_relu_mean - .28209479177387814) < 1e-14 print(dc_covariance(dc_y_input), dc_covariance(dc_y_edges)) print("Exact ReLU mean:", .25, "Gaussian approximation:", dc_gaussian_relu_mean) ``` The backward mask in this example is also explicit: the diagonal weights receive gradient $2$, while the two removed connections receive zero data-loss gradient. Their stored parameters have not been erased. A later example can retain them; an optimizer's separate weight decay can still change them. DropConnect is not permanent pruning. Wan et al., [Sections 2.2–3.2 and Algorithms 1–2](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/wan13.pdf), use unscaled masks during training, not the inverted convention of the first example. They sample a different mask for each training example. For a fixed input, a preactivation $z_i=\sum_j M_{ij}W_{ij}x_j$ has $$ \mu_i=q\sum_jW_{ij}x_j,\qquad \sigma_i^2=q(1-q)\sum_jW_{ij}^2x_j^2. $$ At test time their inference algorithm approximates this sum by a Gaussian with those moments, samples preactivations, applies the activation, and averages the resulting activations before the classifier. This accounts for the fact that applying a nonlinearity to the mean is not the same as averaging the nonlinear outputs. It is still an approximation. In the code above, $z=M_1-M_2$ takes values $-1,0,1$; its exact mean ReLU output is $0.25$. A Gaussian with the same mean $0$ and variance $0.5$ gives approximately $0.2821$, while ReLU of the mean gives $0$. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/structured-dropout-2026-10-29/dropconnect-original.png|Original DropConnect graph: full network, sampled connections and an arborescence]] *Albert Senen–Cerda and Jaron Sanders, [Almost Sure Convergence of Dropout Algorithms for Neural Networks, Figure 1](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume26/20-1396/20-1396.pdf#page=2), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The full original figure and caption are retained. Panels (a–b) compare the full graph with a sampled connection mask; panel (c) is the tree-shaped network used in the paper's theoretical analysis. The original caption says “removing” with probability $p$, but the panels and the following paragraph use $p$ as the keep probability. Our equations use $q$ for keeping.* Random zeros do not by themselves reduce the work of a dense matrix multiplication. Per-example connection masks also need a representation and an implementation; a single masked weight matrix shared across the whole batch is a different noise process from the original algorithm. ## Stochastic depth: one gate for a residual branch For a residual block $y=x+F(x)$, stochastic depth samples one gate for the whole branch $F$. If the gate is zero, every coordinate of that branch vanishes together. Elementwise dropout on $F(x)$ can retain one coordinate and remove another; a single branch gate cannot. The original method of Huang et al., [Section 3, Eqs. 2–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1603.09382v3), uses a Bernoulli gate $b_l$ with survival probability $q_l$ for each block and each mini-batch. Its post-activation ResNet block is $\operatorname{ReLU}(x+b_lF(x))$. At test time all branches are active and their outputs are multiplied by $q_l$. When $b_l=0$, the block is an identity under the paper's nonnegative-input assumption: $\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=x$. That statement does not hold for an arbitrary negative input. Modern DropPath implementations often use inverted scaling instead. For a fixed $x$ and fixed branch output $F(x)$, the two conventions are: | Convention | Training, before any final activation | Evaluation | |---|---|---| | Original stochastic depth | $x+bF(x)$ | $x+qF(x)$ | | Inverted branch dropout | $x+bF(x)/q$ | $x+F(x)$ | For $x=(1,2)$, $F(x)=(3,4)$ and $q=0.5$, the original training outputs are $(1,2)$ or $(4,6)$; their mean is $(2.5,4)$. Inverted scaling instead gives $(1,2)$ or $(7,10)$, whose mean is $(4,6)$. The formulas preserve different reference outputs for the same branch weights. After a nonlinear activation, even equality of these preactivation means does not establish equality of mean predictions. ```python import torch sd_x = torch.tensor([1., 2.], dtype=torch.float64) sd_branch = torch.tensor([3., 4.], dtype=sd_x.dtype) sd_gates = torch.tensor([0., 1.], dtype=sd_x.dtype)[:, None] sd_original = sd_x + sd_gates * sd_branch sd_inverted = sd_x + sd_gates * sd_branch / .5 torch.testing.assert_close(sd_original.mean(0), sd_x + .5 * sd_branch) torch.testing.assert_close(sd_inverted.mean(0), sd_x + sd_branch) sd_coordinate_dropout = sd_x + torch.tensor([1., 0.]) * sd_branch / .5 assert sd_coordinate_dropout.tolist() == [7., 2.] assert not torch.any(torch.all(sd_inverted == sd_coordinate_dropout, dim=1)) print(sd_original, sd_inverted, sd_coordinate_dropout) ``` The original function below is from Ross Wightman's [timm implementation, pinned revision beabdc3a](https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models/blob/beabdc3a6833d39814c895b2bc84cbc61a05834d/timm/layers/drop.py#L157-L175). It uses inverted scaling by default. Its name also avoids confusing branch dropping with the independent connection masks of DropConnect. The function is reproduced unchanged under [Apache 2.0](/licenses/timm-beabdc3a-Apache-2.0.txt); the calls after it are executable examples. ```python import torch from itertools import product def drop_path(x, drop_prob: float = 0., training: bool = False, scale_by_keep: bool = True): """Drop paths (Stochastic Depth) per sample (when applied in main path of residual blocks). This is the same as the DropConnect impl I created for EfficientNet, etc networks, however, the original name is misleading as 'Drop Connect' is a different form of dropout in a separate paper... See discussion: https://github.com/tensorflow/tpu/issues/494#issuecomment-532968956 ... I've opted for changing the layer and argument names to 'drop path' rather than mix DropConnect as a layer name and use 'survival rate' as the argument. """ if drop_prob == 0. or not training: return x keep_prob = 1 - drop_prob shape = (x.shape[0],) + (1,) * (x.ndim - 1) # work with diff dim tensors, not just 2D ConvNets random_tensor = x.new_empty(shape).bernoulli_(keep_prob) if keep_prob > 0.0 and scale_by_keep: random_tensor.div_(keep_prob) return x * random_tensor torch.manual_seed(29) sd_values = torch.ones(16, 3, 4) # [batch, positions, features] sd_masked = drop_path(sd_values, .5, training=True) assert torch.equal(sd_masked, sd_masked[:, :1, :1].expand_as(sd_values)) assert torch.all((sd_masked == 0) | (sd_masked == 2)) assert set(sd_masked[:, 0, 0].tolist()) == {0., 2.} assert drop_path(sd_values, .5, training=False) is sd_values assert torch.count_nonzero(drop_path(sd_values, 1., training=True)) == 0 # Original paper's depth schedule, with independent gates across four blocks. sd_keep = 1 - torch.arange(1, 5, dtype=torch.float64) / 4 * (1 - .5) sd_masks = torch.tensor(list(product([0., 1.], repeat=4)), dtype=sd_keep.dtype) sd_probabilities = torch.where(sd_masks.bool(), sd_keep, 1 - sd_keep).prod(1) sd_depths = sd_masks.sum(1) sd_expected_depth = sd_probabilities @ sd_depths torch.testing.assert_close(sd_probabilities.sum(), torch.tensor(1., dtype=sd_keep.dtype)) assert sd_expected_depth.item() == 2.75 print("Keep probabilities:", sd_keep, "Expected active branches:", sd_expected_depth) ``` For a tensor shaped $[B,T,d]$, the mask has shape $[B,1,1]$: each batch example gets its own gate, shared across all its positions and features. The original paper instead shares a block gate across the mini-batch. Neither is an independent gate per token. With `scale_by_keep=False`, this function returns the unscaled training branch, but its evaluation path still returns the input; that flag alone does not implement the original paper's test-time factor $q$. The depth schedule in the example follows the paper: $q_l=1-\frac lL(1-q_L)$. Linearity of expectation gives $\mathbb E[\text{active branches}]=\sum_{l=1}^Lq_l$. For four branches and $q_L=0.5$, the survival probabilities are $(0.875,0.75,0.625,0.5)$, so the mean active depth is $2.75$. For the paper's $L=54$ residual blocks, it is $40.25$. Active depth is not automatically a runtime reduction. The original mini-batch gate can be sampled before evaluating $F$, allowing the whole branch to be skipped. In `x + drop_path(F(x), ...)`, the argument `F(x)` has already been computed before `drop_path` runs. Multiplying it by zero saves no branch forward computation. Per-example masks require additional conditional execution to skip work for individual examples; normalization statistics can also differ from skipping the whole batch. The attention and embedding variants occur later on the reading route, in [[00 Учебник/05 Attention и Transformer/03 Полный Transformer#transformer-dropout|the complete Transformer]]. There the attention mask forbids connections structurally, while dropout randomly removes some allowed attention weights during training. ## Как шум меняет обучающую цель

The attention and embedding variants occur later on the reading route, in [[00 Учебник/05 Attention и Transformer/03 Полный Transformer#transformer-dropout|the complete Transformer]]. There the attention mask forbids connections structurally, while dropout randomly removes some allowed attention weights during training. ## Источники
